title: Bread on the waters
hookLine: cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days (Ecclesiastes 11:1)
tomorrow: the Preacher's last poem: a house falling quiet. whose house?
last: LEARN AND PRACTICE · THAT IS KNOWLEDGE · EXAMINE MYSELF

lines: CAST THY BREAD UPON THE WATERS.
cards: You hold a door, push a stranger's stalled car to the curb, leave a big tip in a town you're only driving through. You'll never know how any of those stories ends.
Near the close of Ecclesiastes, after all the breath and the circling sun, the Preacher gives a strange piece of advice: "Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days."

teach.b: Bread on a river looks like waste. Readers have heard it two ways. Some hear trade: send your grain out on ships, and in time it comes back.
Others, Jewish and Christian readers alike, hear generosity: give where you can't see the return. Either way, the next lines lean on not knowing.

teach.h: A PORTION TO SEVEN, AND TO EIGHT.
teach.b: "Give a portion to seven, and also to eight; for thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth."

teach.h: WHOEVER WATCHES THE WIND WON'T SOW.
teach.b: Whoever keeps watching the wind, Qoheleth says, never sows. "In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that."
Here's the teaching, and it's a turn in this book.

teach.h: NOT KNOWING IS THE REASON TO GIVE.
teach.b: Hevel, life's brevity and our not knowing, isn't a reason to hold back.

It's the reason to scatter. You can't control which good thing lands, so do more than one, morning and evening. One to tell a friend tonight: in Ecclesiastes, uncertainty is an argument for generosity, not against it.

how: Ecclesiastes 11:1 is quoted in Jewish and Christian settings as a call to generosity; some readers take it as advice about sea trade. Either way the passage stresses acting without knowing the outcome.

games.q: what does “bread on the waters” mean?
o: feed the ducks and fish as a kindness to animals
waste what you have on things that will sink
give freely, since you can't know which gift will land

games.q: the week, and the bread: tap the pairs.
p: no shifted anger, no repeated fault
told to allow what he didn't know
give, not knowing which will prosper

s: 'cast thy bread upon the waters' promises a sure return
the lines after it stress that you don't know which will prosper.
the Preacher says whoever keeps watching the wind won't sow
waiting for perfect conditions means never sowing at all.
readers agree the verse is only about charity
some hear sea trade, some hear generosity; both lean on not knowing.

games.q: you have a little to give and three causes asking. you can't tell which will do the most good. what does Ecclesiastes 11 say?
o: give a portion to seven, and also to eight: spread it, since you can't know.
wait until you're sure which one works, then give it all there.
give nothing: if it's all hevel, nothing will come of it anyway.
games.why: 'thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that': the Preacher turns not knowing into a reason to sow morning and evening.

practice: Do one small giving now, where you'll never see the result: put a coin or a note aside for the next tip jar, leave a kind unsigned note for a neighbor, set a book by the door to leave where someone will find it.
Let it go like bread on moving water. Don't follow it with your eyes; let the current have it.
